metric1_population_workforce_gap.title: Elderly Population vs. Caregiver Supply Gap
metric1_population_workforce_gap.subtitle: The structural pressure behind every use case: care demand is rising while the workforce that delivers it is not keeping pace

population_series.label: People needing care (Pflegebeduerftige, millions)
population_series.source: Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), press release PD24_478_224 (Dec 2024); federal government mid-century projection cited in market_research.md §1.1

workforce_series.label: Care workforce, ambulatory + residential (millions)
workforce_series.source: Destatis Pflegestatistik 2023 (1.264M employed in ambulatory + residential care, May 2023 release PD23_N029_23); Destatis press release PD24_033_23_12 (Jan 2024) projects at least +280,000 additional care workers needed by 2049, shown here as implied workforce requirement

Germany.callout: Deutscher Pflegerat projects a separate, larger shortfall of up to 500,000 care workers by 2034 (cited in market_research.md §1.2) — the gap widens faster under this estimate than the Destatis 280k/2049 figure shown in the chart.

population_series.label: Population of pensionable age (millions)
population_series.source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), National Population Projections, 2024-based

workforce_series.label: Adult social care workforce, England (millions)
workforce_series.source: Skills for Care, 'The State of the Adult Social Care Sector and Workforce in England 2024'

United Kingdom.callout: Skills for Care reports an 8.3% vacancy rate (~131,000 unfilled posts) in 2024 — roughly 3x the wider economy's vacancy rate. No published workforce projection to 2034 was found, so the workforce series shows a single current data point against the rising population trend.

population_series.label: Population aged 85+ (millions)
population_series.source: U.S. Census Bureau, 'Demographic Turning Points for the United States' (2020) population projections

workforce_series.label: Direct care workforce (millions)
workforce_series.source: PHI (Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute), 'Direct Care Workers in the United States: Key Facts 2025'

United States.callout: Unlike Germany and the UK, the US direct care workforce more than doubled 2014–2024 — yet PHI projects 6.1 million home care job openings by 2034, driven primarily by turnover (median wage $17.36/hr, 2024). The gap here is retention, not headcount growth. Note the population series (2030/2040) and workforce series (2014/2024) cover different periods due to data availability — shown together to illustrate direction, not a single trend line.

metric1_population_workforce_gap.note: Time periods differ by country due to data availability from national statistical agencies. Each series is independently sourced and dated; the chart is intended to show directional divergence (rising demand vs. constrained supply), not a precisely aligned cross-country index.

metric2_ai_adoption.title: AI Adoption in Elderly / Home Care — Germany vs. UK vs. US
metric2_ai_adoption.subtitle: Germany is behind, but the broader market is moving fast — this is a catch-up investment, not a leap into the unknown

bars.metric_definition: % of home care industry leaders already using or planning to use AI for operations management
bars.source: AxisCare 2026 Home Care Industry Survey (400+ industry leaders, June 2026)

bars.metric_definition: % of adult social care providers using at least one care technology (digital records, sensors, monitoring, video, apps — not AI-specific)
bars.source: DHSC / Digital Care Hub, 'Technology Use in Adult Social Care: 2025 Survey Results' (1,085 providers)
bars.specificity: Care-sector specific, but broad digital technology — NOT an AI-only figure

bars.metric_definition: % of German companies (all sectors) actively using AI, up from 9% in 2022
bars.specificity: General business, all sectors — not care-specific. A separate CEPR (Feb 2026) survey finds 56% of German firms using or planning to use generative AI specifically.

metric2_ai_adoption.note: These figures are NOT directly comparable — each measures something different (AI in home care operations vs. broad care technology vs. general-business AI adoption). They are presented together deliberately, in the spirit of this project's evidence-credibility approach: Germany's care sector has no published AI-specific adoption survey, so the closest available figures are shown with their definitions made explicit. The honest takeaway is directional: AI/digital adoption in care-adjacent contexts is substantial and growing in the UK and US, while Germany's general AI adoption (20–56%) still trails — supporting the 'catching up, not leading into the unknown' framing.
